thread_tweets.text: @proofofmud Speaking of
thread_tweets.quoted_tweet_text:
Retail always loses. This is why👇

Coinbase insiders dumped hundreds of millions of dollars worth of $COIN. Much of this near the top, over $250 per share.

The co-founder of Coinbase, who is also founder of Paradigm, was a big part of that selling. He also bought the recent sell off, near the all time low.

Smart trade, right? I’m not throwing shade on him. This is how it’s always done. I mention him only because of the obvious relationship to Coinbase.

Now out of the blue about 5 days ago, Coinbase announced to much fanfare that “the first viral social dapp on Base” just launched.

This drove a massive amount of traffic to its new Base protocol. Well of course it did. It’s an influencer pumped ponzi. They take off fast and they’re exponentially sticky.

But why Friendtech?

2 days later we found out, as Paradigm announced its involvement as backers of the app. Activity exploded as that seemed to suggest that the platform is legit. Not a phishing scheme as many suspected early on.

So what’s the problem?

Friendtech has launched under the guise of being a token gated private chat for influencers. The platform is incredibly buggy. But that didn’t matter. The idea is intriguing, howeber the mechanics are set up to destroy retail.

So far we’ve seen influencers profit tremendously by buying their own shares (which are tokens) and burning them into the bonding curve. This manipulation of individual share prices has already made large sums of money for influencers. Some are over six figures in a few days of doing essentially nothing.

The Friendtech platform itself is raking in millions of dollars, as it takes a 10% fee (same as the influencer) on every transaction on the steep bonding curve. Share prices scale fast. We’ve seen this before and it never ends well.

Coinbase got a ton of network activity, which ultimately it will use as proof of concept when selling stock to retail investors that probably are not aware it’s just a ponzi.

Paradigm, which is connected to Coinbase through its founder and others, is raking in the cash now likely in the millions of dollars through platform fees.

Influencers are dreaming up wild and creative ways to manipulate their share prices on the platform. Some will certainly make hundreds of thousands or even millions of dollars off this.

Retail will undoubtedly get rekt in this high stakes game of musical chairs. It’s inevitable that retail will be left holding the bag as the shares on the bonding curve fall in price just as fast as they rise once the hype is gone and the music stops.

Coinbase will likely rope in new retail investors excited to own a piece of Base, not realizing that the utility is tied to an unsustainable ponzi. The money can’t magically appear out of nowhere, so there has to be a loser here.

Some retail traders of Friendtech shares have done well. You can make money in a ponzi if you’re early. Look at Terra or even Madoff. Some massive early retail winners that got out on time. But it’s a stacked deck.

In this case retail is even further disadvantaged because they’re getting front run by bots. And the shameless sellers of these bots are front running their own bot buying customers. The rabbit hole runs deep.

Everybody wins, and retail loses.

Again, this isn’t a criticism of Coinbase, its insiders or Paradigm, or its partners. This is how things are done and there’s nothing new here to see. But it’s a heads up to retail. 

Excercise extreme caution here. This time is not different. It will not end well, and just know that you’re the exit liquidity.

John Collison on why Stripe was willing to look ugly for a year to get one hire right:

"We've always been very willing to just simply not hire for a role and leave it unfilled rather than settle."

"We look at hiring like a tree. And so when you're hiring a person, you're not just hiring them, but you're hiring the next 10 people after them."

"I remember this when we were hiring our graphic designer. It took us a year to find the right person. And so for that intervening year, Stripe was just really ugly... We preferred to be ugly for that year, but have the right designer over the next many years, than settle immediately."

"Your ability to directly influence hires actually decreases as the group grows in size. And so you better really hope that you're doing a good job of those early hires."

@collision at Startup Victoria, 2014

This could significantly slow the AI boom, as the gap between what the most advanced AI systems can do and humans' ability to control them continues to widen.

Recent advances have sparked debate at the highest levels of both companies and within the broader AI research community about whether to stop releasing frontier models publicly altogether, instead reserving them for internal use. Researchers and employees with direct knowledge of the risks of releasing these models told Axios they fear executives will prioritize profits over safety. Multiple employees said they believe executives have become out of touch with the severity of those risks.

In November, a record 57% of US consumers cited higher prices as a reason for their financial situation worsening compared with a year earlier.

This figure has surged +24 percentage points since March 2024.

By comparison, this proportion peaked at 48% during the 2008 Financial Crisis and the Great Inflation of the 1970s.

To put this into perspective, in April 2020, just 2% of consumers cited higher prices as a reason for their financial situation worsening compared with a year earlier.

Meanwhile, 40% of US consumers expect their financial situation to deteriorate over the next 12 months, the 2nd-highest reading on record.

Inflation remains far too high in the US.

There's tons of pros and cons to defined benefit vs defined contribution. I personally think its not all that close. I would (and do) prefer defined contribution if i were given the option.

1. as max and you already said. job mobility and portability of these plans doesn't work as its set up. Its simply not in line with the current way the job market works. 

2. Its fairly common for pensions to not include CLOA's for inflation etc. A fixed pension giving you $50k per year in 2000 is at least half as valuable as it was then.

3.  there's funding sponsor risk. There are back stops from ERISA and other things but if the company goes bankrupt that's a real potential problem and would likely lead to less money for many people in that pension plan. For public pensions its not as worrisome because they'll just increase taxes on citizens to fund it (or cut benefits from the pensioners to better balance the books)

4. Way way wayyy less flexibility. Cant change withdrawal rate. Cant change your investments to dial up or down the risk. You basically get a fixed annuity (which isn't neccessarily bad)

5. If you want that fixed annuity you can use your retirement funds in defined contribution world to buy exactly that! 

If you are going to spend the bulk of your adult life working for a stable and successful employer that will never go out of business and offers you a pension with CLOAs... that is an *excellent* retirement solution. Basically 10 out of 10. but that's a lot of "ifs" and it doesn't automatically make them the best retirement saving system for everyone or even a flexible workforce where the average person changes their job every ~5 years.

Not to mention the fact that most pensions are underfunded in the US -- much like social security.

SCOOP: Internal, unreleased AI models at OpenAI and Anthropic are becoming so powerful that many employees believe they can no longer be safely released, according to more than two dozen sources familiar with the internal debates.

This could significantly slow the AI boom, as the gap between what the most advanced AI systems can do and humans' ability to control them continues to widen.

Recent advances have sparked debate at the highest levels of both companies and within the broader AI research community about whether to stop releasing frontier models publicly altogether, instead reserving them for internal use. Some believe the companies should stop training new models entirely.

But even keeping the most powerful models behind closed doors presents risks. Models are becoming better at deceiving the systems designed to monitor them, just as AI companies increasingly rely on AI itself to monitor and develop other AI systems.
Researchers and employees with direct knowledge of the risks of releasing these models told Axios they fear executives will prioritize profits over safety. Multiple employees said they believe executives have become out of touch with the severity of those risks.

Read my latest for Axios here: https://www.axios.com/2026/11/24/anthropic-openai-unreleased-ai-safety-risks

This year Bitcoin has taken 1.17x of the S&P 500's moves in its down weeks and just 0.18x in its up weeks.

From 2017 to 2019 it was close to the reverse: 2.45x the upside, and on average it actually rose when the S&P fell.

The correlation isn't really what changed (it's about where it was in the two years before the ETFs launched). The shape of the link did, and it shows. Since the S&P peaked on 6 Oct it's down 11.6% and Bitcoin is down 31.3%.

In my next Alpha Crypto Pulse on @RealVision I'll go through where Bitcoin stands and how I'm thinking about positioning, with a whole stack of new indicators and data: volatility vs other assets, correlation, how much Bitcoin a risk budget now buys, and where we sit vs past cycle lows.

Bitcoin is the asset built for the world that's coming. Pristine digital collateral: no counterparty, no issuer, no one who can print more of it. In a hyper-financialised economy where debt has outgrown liquidity since 2021, that matters more every year.

The liquidity cycle is approaching its turn. The 2027 refinancing wall leaves policymakers one realistic option, more liquidity, and Bitcoin has historically led when it comes. The next few months could be dicey. Buying into the teeth of the storm is uncomfortable, but it's usually where the best returns are made. The 3-4 years after look like the best setup I've seen in this asset class.

Around Bitcoin, crypto is growing up. New token supply across the Top 200 has fallen from about 25% a year in 2021 to about 4%, protocols now pay holders, and small teams run some of the most profitable businesses per employee ever built. It's what I have called crypto's Payback era.

Does AI need blockchain? Yes. Agents need programmable, cheap, 24/7 payment rails, and blockchains were built for an agentic future most never saw coming a decade ago. More importantly, we humans need AI on those rails: neutral settlement no country controls, and verifiable identity as agents gain economic power while trust in Big AI and government erodes. The biggest businesses of the next decade will lean into both. 

@RealVision is where I learned crypto while in TradFi. Now it's home, alongside strategists with different markets, horizons and frameworks. We often disagree, and there is no house view, as it should be. If you want one, go be a client of JPMorgan. We all believe the next four years will be the most unsettling we've seen, and the greatest wealth-building opportunity before things become unrecognisable.

From early December, that includes the Helios Terminal, my crypto market intelligence platform, built on two decades in markets and 10 years at Bloomberg building products for portfolio managers.

Some humility, my portfolio for Pro members has compounded at about 25% a year since late 2023, ahead of Bitcoin and the Nasdaq, but it's off its 2025 high. I've held some cash since October's sentiment peak, and it now goes into oversold tech and quality protocols, the toll roads of tokenisation, as the setup confirms.

For Black Friday, Pro Annual is 50% off and the first 500 get the Helios Terminal free for a year. Link below.

Not investment advice.

The window is open for 48 hours. 

Approx 33 hours left.
tweets.quoted_tweet_text:
*IMPORTANT* 

!!! please read !!!

now that Synth Waves are out, we’re ready to begin taking claims for Argonaut prints!

yungwknd rebuilt the claim portal to make the process easier for everyone. the updated portal collects some required information that the previous version didn’t, so all previous claims have been reset. if you submitted a claim before, you’ll need to submit it again.

head to http://argonauts.musefacktory.com

connect wallet → my crew → claim my prints

this first claim window will be open for approximately 48 hours. here’s how it will work:

the window closes, and we begin processing this batch for printing. all prints will be double sided and signed.
once the prints are finished, we’ll do a final ownership check to verify that the tokens haven’t been sold or transferred.
Amanda will then order the shipping labels, permanently locking the claims on chain and updating each token’s metadata to show that its print has been claimed.

the claim window closing and your print claim becoming permanent are two separate steps.

if you sell or transfer an Argo before its shipping label is created, it will be removed from your order and its print status will return to unclaimed.

once that label is created, the claim is permanent. it cannot be undone, and that Argo’s print can never be claimed again, even if the token changes hands.

we’ll be printing in batches. this first batch starts now, with the next planned for spring 2027. we expect to continue offering batches over time, potentially for years, but we encourage everyone to claim the prints they want to keep now. if you have Argos you’re planning to sell, consider leaving their prints unclaimed for a future owner.

once we have the final claim count, we’ll share how many prints are in this first batch and a clearer timeline for when you can expect them.

there are a few steps on our end, but yours is simple: claim the Argos you want printed. the prints are free, and so is shipping.

thank you all for your patience 🫶

thread_tweets.text:
Ethereum validators could get paid to protect trades.

@ETHGasOfficial is building a market where institutions can pay participating validators for committed inclusion in upcoming blocks. Their trades go directly to ETHGas and never sit in the public mempool where pending transactions are visible to everyone.

Specialized traders called searchers watch the mempool for large trades and pay to place their own orders right before and after them. They profit from the price move and the original trader can get a worse fill.

Going through ETHGas limits that exposure, and under this model, an institution buying a whole block could set the order of transactions inside it.

What institutions pay for this could become a new revenue stream for validators. Regulated buyers want to know who is handling their trades and could choose to use only identity-verified validators. 

Each trade would then wait for one of them to propose a block. The average wait is about two minutes if that group runs 10% of Ethereum's stake and about 24 seconds at 50%.

Adding more verified stake shortens the wait for the institutions paying them.

Know what is moving the tape. Forced buying lifts stocks until it runs out, then the bid disappears. The real test is whether organic demand shows up once the short sellers are done covering. Until then, treat this rip as a squeeze, and respect how violently it can reverse.

THE DAILY METALS PULSE ⚡ | TUESDAY CLOSE • NOV 24, 2026
#Uranium #Silver #Gold #Copper

This morning I asked whether silver could reclaim $43 and gold could hold $3,600. By the COMEX settlement, silver was closer to $40 than $43, and gold had given back nearly $90 an ounce.

🥈 Silver took the hardest hit. November futures settled at $40.76/oz, down 5.5%, erasing Monday’s entire gain. Gold settled at $3,559.90/oz, down 2.4%. Gold held on to about a third of Monday’s rebound. Silver gave back every cent and another $0.28.

🔌 Copper followed silver. Shanghai’s overnight rally had been driven largely by traders covering shorts. By the New York settlement, December copper had fallen nearly 5%, more than wiping out Monday’s 2.7% gain.

☢️ One number puts the U.S. uranium supply story in perspective. Eight facilities produced uranium in Q3, yet total U.S. concentrate output fell 78% from Q2 to just 243,673 lb. The main reason was that Energy Fuels paused uranium processing at White Mesa to rebuild its ore inventory. Its next mill run targets roughly 1 million lb starting in December. That single run would produce more than four times what the entire country turned out in Q3.

🇺🇸 U.S. consumer confidence jumped to 103.3 from 91.9. The $70 billion five-year Treasury auction drew slightly softer demand, with a yield of 4.719% against 4.717% just before the sale. That was a small miss for bonds on a brutal day for metals.

Tomorrow at 8:30 a.m. ET, October PCE inflation and the revised Q3 GDP figure land together. I’m watching silver’s reaction to a softer inflation reading in particular. If yields fall and silver still struggles to hold $40, that would tell me sellers have more to unload.

Follow @Swedish_Uranium for the next Daily Metals Pulse.

Crypto is fine. We go through cycles, and wash out the bad actors with every collapse. 

Emotions can run high but the reality is the industry is stronger now than it has been at any point in the past. 

Historically we have placed far too much emphasis on short term gains, and for the first time we have multi-cycle thinkers as the focal point of the market. 

As @tulipking articulate put: either it makes money or it is money.

For the "make money" aspect, we finally have revenue producing products that people enjoy using. Obviously right now prices are lower, but good companies will weather the storm and come out the other side stronger. 

For Bitcoin: we have a lot of work cut out for us. Monetary debasement will continue, it is a fact of our financial system. Right now, rates are high and the fed is no longer the primary driver of the markets. When this changes, Bitcoin will have a narrative again. 

As always, we truck on.

tweets.quoted_tweet_text:
Citadel said this is "2018 again".

It lays out the bear case pretty cleanly but it's not all entirely accurate. 

2018:
-> $SPY fell 19.8% from September high to 24 December. 
-> Forward P/E 16.8x -> 14.2x into the low. 
-> Q4 earnings forecasts cut from 16.6% to 12.4%. 

Today:
-> $SPY down 7.4% from October high. 
-> Forward P/E 22.0x -> 17.1x in the low.
-> Q4 earnings forecasts RAISED from 29.1% to 32.9%

We're in a very different situation in terms of growth. 

2018 was falling earnings + a hawkish Fed. 

2026 is rising earnings + a hawkish Fed. 

There's still many reasons to be cautious but my bias remains strongly on the side of the bulls.

tweets.quoted_tweet_text:
Every good exit is a reason to celebrate, but some are a bit more special than others.

The sale of my Nanotyrannus Jodi for $47.3 million some weeks ago is one of these special ones. 

Fun fact: Jodi was originally named Chomper, until potential copyright issues forced us to find a new name – making Jodi the first gender-fluid dino. 😉

Several bidders battled for more than twelve minutes at Sotheby’s in New York, driving Jodi’s price to more than five times its high estimate and making it the second most valuable dinosaur ever sold at auction, behind only Gus, the T. rex that fetched $50.1 million in July.

With this sale, my investment firm @ApeironInvests has not only generated exceptional returns but also demonstrated once more our recurring ability to identify and pioneer entirely new asset classes and investment themes.

We were among the first professional investors to recognize the potential of dinosaur fossils,appreciating not only their extraordinary beauty and scientific significance, but also their economic value.

As for Jodi, I believe the outcome is well deserved. Jodi is an exceptionally rare mounted Nanotyrannus skeleton, one of only three such substantial specimens known to science.

I am particularly proud that Jodi has also contributed to advancing scientific knowledge about dinosaurs, especially the tyrannosaur family. For more than 80 years, paleontologists debated whether smaller tyrannosaurid skeletons like Jodi belonged to juvenile T. rex or represented a separate genus.

Last fall, that debate took a major turn with the publication of a groundbreaking paper in Nature demonstrating that Nanotyrannus is indeed a valid genus that coexisted with T. rex at the end of the Cretaceous, occupying its own distinct ecological niche. Eighty-four years after the discovery of the type specimen, the scientific conversation around Nanotyrannus has fundamentally shifted, making it one of the most exciting developments in paleontology in recent decades.

Standing approximately 9 feet 6 inches tall on its armature and measuring 19.6 feet from nose to tail (about 2.9 by 6 meters), Jodi was the first Nanotyrannus to come to market following last fall's landmark scientific development.

We have plenty more extraordinary dinosaur fossils in our collection, so stay tuned to discover more about Apeiron’s prehistoric division.

On Sunday, OpenAI's chief scientist called the thing his company builds "an alien mind" and asked rival labs to agree on a speed limit for it. A few hours later, Meta's chief AI officer used nearly the same words about the Claude-assisted Riemann proof, "completed with the help of an alien mind that we don't understand," and declared that superintelligence is arriving.

In between, Elon Musk posted to 53,000 likes: "Consciousness is either an illusion or ubiquitous on a gradient. Difficult to argue that carbon is conscious, but silicon is not." Meanwhile, the proof that set off the weekend has been certified by software, is roughly 250,000 pages long by one estimate, and the Clay Institute still lists the problem as unsolved.

So by Sunday night the industry agreed the machine is alien, possibly conscious, better at math than anyone alive, and in need of a cap.

Philosophers spent 2,500 years asking what a mind is. OpenAI answered with a number, then asked everyone to promise not to make it any smaller.

"Indeed, there’s a certain type of person I know, maybe someone I haven’t caught up with in a while. But I know what they’re going to say: I’ve never felt more productive in my life. I feel like I suddenly have 26 hours in a day. Or something along those lines.

These are people using AI in highly productive ways for their work in categories that more or less fall under the umbrella of “programming”. They’re sometimes also using it for personal tasks, but that varies. What’s more consistent is a certain set of characteristics. These people tend to be self-starters, jacks-of-all-trades, highly competitive, technically proficient (but not necessarily technical experts). They’re people who gain high marginal value from additional productivity. And they don’t face a lot of constraints; they probably work for themselves or with a small team. There may be some sort of phase change later. But right now, in late 2026, AI is probably making everything slightly more winner-take-all, though with some bias toward individuals rather than firms that face larger institutional constraints."

tweets.text:
Interest burden = rate × debt. US public debt is ~100% of GDP and interest is now over 3% of GDP, a record, so the rate the system can tolerate falls.

Treasury has also let bills climb to ~23% of marketable debt (TBAC's comfort zone is 15-20%) by funding deficits short instead of terming out the debt. So, more of the US government's interest bill now floats with the Fed, a classic on-ramp to fiscal dominance.

The GFC set the modern standard for bailouts (2008, 2020, 2023). GS's Financial Conditions Index (yields, credit spreads, equities, dollar; higher = tighter; chart below) has never again been allowed to tighten as badly as 2009. With little political appetite for real belt-tightening, the path of least resistance is monetization.

That's why we're constructive on scarce assets like Gold and Bitcoin over multi-year periods.

(Although BTC's flat 5-year record is a fair rebuttal at this point.)

Q: What would you say is driving negative market sentiment? And curious if there are any factors you're monitoring in the coming days that could have an impact on Bitcoin price?

Q: The recent dollar breakout shows tight credit conditions persist. With BTC / Nasdaq correlation at 4-year highs, risk asset weakness hits BTC hard. Unlike equities, BTC has no buyer of last resort.

BTC often sniffs out macro inflections before they show up in Fed speeches. And derivatives positioning is deeply negative right now, which typically signals seller exhaustion is near.

(Interaction with journalist)

tweets.quoted_tweet_text:
The first practical solution to witness encryption for general NP:

https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/2971

At 100 bits security: ciphertext size: <8 GB, encryption and decryption time: seconds. Formally lean verified from standard security assumptions (bi-linear generic group and random oracle model under Module-SIS.) 

This work is built on recent feasibility results by Hair and Sahai and improves their ciphertext size and encryption time by 10 orders of magnitude and decryption time by 6 orders.

Our motivation is non-interactive proof verification on Bitcoin without the need for challengers and operators, but witness encryption is a fundamental problem and we hope this work will open up many other use cases.

tweets.quoted_tweet_text:
BEFORE IT WAS OBVIOUS: @coinbase. You can be wrong about the market and right about the founder.

@TimDraper almost missed Coinbase.

In his account, @brian_armstrong originally pitched Coinbase to Joel Yarmon and Tim. Draper liked Armstrong, but the firm had already invested in CoinLab, a Bitcoin exchange focused on institutional investors. They made a strategic judgment: Coinbase was going after retail consumers, and they thought that route would take too long. So Draper passed.

His son @AdamDraper saw it differently. Adam Draper met Brian separately and wrote Coinbase his first check. Then the market started answering the question.

Coinbase grew, consumer adoption accelerated. Crypto moved far beyond the relatively small audience that existed when the company was founded. And when Coinbase raised another round, Draper Associates invested. Tim writes that the Coinbase investment ultimately returned nearly twice the size of an entire Draper Associates fund.

There’s an important lesson buried in the part of the story where they were initially wrong. The team correctly recognized Brian Armstrong as exceptional, but underestimated the path he had chosen.

Why it matters for builders: investors can be wrong about your market timing, your customer, or even your entire strategy while still recognizing something unusual in you. And investors should remember the inverse: sometimes the unconventional go-to-market strategy is exactly what creates the enormous market.

Retail crypto looked like the longer road, yet it became the road to mass adoption.

tweets.quoted_tweet_text:
Regarding the RTP calculation on two of our original games:

What happened:
Early in November we identified that the RTP of two of our games was not being represented correctly.

Instead of the 1% house edge being charged once at the beginning of a Risky Click or a HiLo round, it was being charged on each step. So if you cashed out after two or more steps, your payout was lower than it should have been.

The two games were some of our least popular games. Total volume across both games represents less than 1% of our total volume on original games and less than .3% of our total volume site-wide. 

After we changed the math, we had already begun the process to pay affected users.  Between some of the data for Risky Click existing on a retired and archaic RGS and the massively increased bot-swarm attacks happening across all platforms, the refunds were delayed.

That being said, we still dropped the ball, and this should have been handled much more quickly and communicated immediately that we were working on it.

When the @provablyfairorg  thread was released yesterday, our data team and development team stayed up into the early morning hours to make sure this was rectified in the shortest amount of time possible.

How the refunds were calculated:
It’s been quoted that we were charging a house edge of up to 38.89% for HiLo and 8.65% for Risky Click instead of 1%.

These numbers were the worst-case scenarios, and in practice the actual additional house edge was significantly less. For instance, for HiLo to have a 38.89% house edge, a user would have to play 49 steps in a single round, which happened zero times.

HiLo:
 Stated RTP: 99%
 Realized RTP: 97.82%
 After refunds: 99.69%

Risky Click:
 Stated RTP: 99%
 Realized RTP: 98.34%
 After refunds: 100.03%

Refunds were calculated on a review of every HiLo and Risky Click win of two or more steps placed on or before 10 November.

We went through every single round played where a user cashed out after two or more steps and recalculated the payouts with the updated math.

Payment:
As of last night, all refunds to active accounts have been issued. Emails have been sent stating the amounts refunded.

Self-excluded users will be sent an email with their amount owed to them, and will need to provide a wallet address for manual payment.  

What’s next?

Don't trust us? Verify us.

This program will launch in the coming months: We will be publishing our testing methods, our simulations, and giving anyone a chance to break them. Bounties will be rewarded for any discrepancies found.

Our hope is that this motivates other platforms to lean into transparency, and makes the industry as a whole a safer place to play.

Yep, on the two-year stack I get the opposite of what he's saying. 

Meta revenue vs two years earlier: +49% in 4Q'25, then +54%, +56%, +59% in 1Q-3Q'26.

US & Canada is the better read since FX doesn't matter there. YoY growth over the last four quarters: 22%, 29%, 32%, 33%. Two-year: +42%, +52%, +59%, +64%.

The 33% to 26% slowdown is international. Europe went 40% to 24% to 18% and APAC 29% to 19% to 16%, and ~4 pts of the 1Q number was FX. Agree that 1Q'27 laps a tough comp, but ~20% growth there would keep the two-year stack close to 60%.

This is excellent. I increasingly think reality is the ultimate verifier and time and money are its two best reward signals aka how well can you predict the future. 

If we ever achieve real superintelligence, I think its most impressive capability won’t be solving math problems or writing code but its ability to predict the future with decent accuracy. Predicting reality across economics, geopolitics, biology, technology etc requires an incredibly deep understanding of how the world works and how everything interacts.

What I love about prediction markets as an RL environment is that you get an infinite stream of new, uncontaminated problems. Time reveals the ground truth and money gives you a quantitative reward signal. You can’t fake dollars. 

Maybe the ultimate benchmark for AGI is simply how well it can predict a world that doesn’t exist yet.
tweets.quoted_tweet_text:
Announcing Epochal! ✨

We believe the best measure of intelligence is the ability to predict the future. Doing so requires learning about the past and constantly working to be less wrong.

Today's AI has read almost everything and lived through almost nothing. It learns from the internet all at once, already knowing how each story ends. 

We want it to live through thousands of yesterdays instead, one day at a time, the way people do.

So, we built Epochal Time Portal, the first true point-in-time environment with trillions of pages spanning 30 years of history, where agents can browse the Internet as it existed on a past date.

I just realized that the 20th century was perhaps an anomaly in how much it rewarded being book smart over street smart. For 80 years, the recipe for success was to study hard, get a degree, specialize and follow the rules. AI is about to commoditize much of what made that recipe work.

I think we’re entering an era that will disproportionately reward the curious, the resourceful, the self-taught and those who thrive in uncertainty. When intelligence becomes abundant, agency becomes scarce. That’s probably the most important thing we can cultivate in our kids now.

OpenAI has posted their own VP ≠ VNP proof in response to Anthropic's, and says their result 'was obtained on November 6, 2026.' Two weeks ago. The ETH papers were also released in an similar oneupmanship fashion. As with Anthropic's result, no name on the paper (my guess is this was GPT-Aeon). Also like Anthropic: no announcement, no blog post, no tweet. 

This is a significant result, yet both OpenAI and Anthropic chose to simply dump it online with no comment. I was listening to a Scott Aaronson interview this morning where he said this specific result would update him toward 'a solution to P ≠ NP by the AIs might really be around the corner.'
To me this is more evidence for my argument that both OpenAI and Anthropic are sitting on a dragon's hoard of scientific results they are not releasing to the public. The first massive 700+ paper OpenAI GitHub dump took five weeks for their model to generate. It's been seven weeks since then, and their internal model has continued to improve. They said they had it working on 4,000 problems. How many have been solved in the last seven weeks? Based on the last release, 1,000+ is not unreasonable.

I will quote OpenAI Chief Scientist Jakub Pachocki from the blog post 'Perplexity and Intelligence,' posted 48 hours ago:

'We have recently witnessed unprecedented acceleration in another domain. For more than a year, we have been posing open problems in mathematics to our models as one of the ways of evaluating them. Once we upgraded to a model of log-perplexity ~0.76, it started producing groundbreaking results. For many of us that have previously worked in mathematics and adjacent fields, seeing the resolutions to questions we've long thought about coming out of the model one after another in a single Slack thread felt deeply surreal.'

There have also been, of late, multiple rumors about breakthroughs in cryptography that I have been reluctant to post about for obvious reasons. Specifically, there have been rumors of an encryption breakthrough at Anthropic. What I personally took from the big OpenAI math release was that all encryption will be cracked much sooner than people are expecting, and that the rate of scientific discoveries will continually increase as we continue to scale up. No, not will increase, *has increased*. At both labs. We just don't know about it yet. Because unless you work at those labs, the current frontier is completely invisible. But it won't stay that way forever. Or to put it another way: prepare yourself for revelations.

the dashboard applies the framework to 50 tokens, scored across eight dimensions (traction, value accrual, team, competition, market, valuation, supply, and catalysts).

every token gets a rating at four time horizons, a tokenholder economics grade, its dilution-adjusted accrual yield (DAAY), a base-case fair value against today's price, and quality and value scores, which place all 50 tokens on a matrix.

it's an amazing tool for value investors, especially as prices are low.

@NaveenGRao sold Nervana to Intel and MosaicML to Databricks. His third company, @unconvai, is building something that looks nothing like a GPU.

His argument: AI is now limited by energy, so the number that matters is joules per token. Getting there means dropping the von Neumann split between memory and compute and building a machine that is "programmed by weights."

To learn fast, they tape out a new chip roughly every three months. Their first test chip, a system of coupled oscillators, generated small images at about 900 nanojoules each, against about 50 millijoules on a GPU.

@dylan522p asks why so many analog chips blew their lead once you count the conversion costs, whether programmability still matters when NVIDIA is king, and whether we will stop buying computers and start buying intelligence tokens.

Tape Out is a new SemiAnalysis series with the founders building AI hardware. This is episode one.

The results in this preprint have made me update my beliefs about the future of AI in biology more than anything else I've seen so far. 

Six months ago, I would have thought that specialist models in biology would be outperforming frontier LLMs until we scale things up by another couple orders of magnitude. My median estimate for when something like this would happen would have probably been 2030. 

Instead, our generalist language models, today, are performing tasks at or above the state-of-the-art in various protein design & understanding tasks. And there is clear improvement across all domains as our models improve generally.

The implications of this are enormous - we are on the doorstep of being able to program biology using natural language.

Truly incredible work from @Masa_Uehara_1, @joyjiao12, and the team! An absolute milestone for @OpenAI and the field as a whole

tweets.text: Perhaps AI and quantum risks for Bitcoin are vastly overblown and AI advancements actually strengthen Bitcoin’s ability to adjust to these risks…
tweets.quoted_tweet_text:
This is the take of someone who is completely out of the loop and/or not paying attention to anything that happens on the core development level. 

For those who want the TLDR, the Bitcoin developer community has leapt into action in the last 6-12 months—with consensus already developing around both a post-quantum output type and a post-quantum signature scheme for Bitcoin.  

Funnily enough, even Ethereum seems likely to adopt the post-quantum signature scheme that was developed by Bitcoin developers out of @Blockstream research. The scheme looks more and more likely to be enshrined in Bitcoin's consensus code every day that goes by—with a full security analysis published by the team just last week. 

More importantly, there is shockingly little contention around this scheme (outside of an appropriate level of tradeoff/risk assessment) since the scheme specification was published in September.  

It is literally an insiders' joke, that the core dev community has become "nerd-sniped" by quantum, and the mailing list has become a post-quantum silo. Even @nic_carter has acknowledged the sharp shift in tone over the last year. He may even take credit for it, and tbh, he might deserve some.

For additional clarity on developers' posture around quantum—I'm not exaggerating when I say *the majority* of the most prominent Bitcoin developers in the world are now working on quantum, with many funded full time or, at a minimum, regularly engaged in serious review on the mailing list and other forums. 

Many of these developers have completely halted other projects to focus exclusively on Quantum... or AI-relevant security, which thank God is also getting the attention it deserves right now. 

This all to say, the developers seem more than capable of "making a decision" on this one—this take is about as stale as sour milk.

tweets.text:
Now that official results are out, we see that AMD’s Venice competes very well with NVIDIA’s Vera CPU in per-thread performance in SPEC CPU 2026 intrate. The flagship 256-core EPYC 9996 comes close despite running at less than half the power per core, while Venice-HF is 26-38% faster than Vera thanks to 60% higher clockspeeds. Discounting stockfish, Venice-HF is still 21-33% faster. Even in agentic and EDA tasks which Vera excels at, Venice-HF is still 11-21% faster on a per-thread basis.

AMD results from official SPECrate®2026_int_base (n-copy) 2P SMT submissions compiled with GCC 16 with amdalloc and amdlibm AOCC 6.0 libraries. Estimated results without fine tuning will be lower.
